This is synthetic evaluation material for a controlled source corpus. It is not documentation of a deployed protocol. An acknowledgement reports that a receiver has observed a message identifier and recorded the associated receipt. The sender can keep that receipt separately from its original payload so that a later retry can be recognized without duplicating application delivery.

Identity and payload integrity answer different questions. A stable identifier describes which logical message is being discussed. A checksum describes which payload bytes were supplied. These concepts are related, but neither alone determines a retry budget, a timeout interval, or a guarantee about network availability. Those choices require a separate protocol specification.

When reviewing captured material, readers should distinguish a definition from an empirical performance result. This introductory note defines acknowledgement terminology only. It makes no numerical claim about attempts, deadlines, throughput, or loss rates. A source that specifies those values should be cited directly when answering a question about them.

This is synthetic evaluation material for a controlled source corpus. The Evaluation Standards Working Group publishes the Harbor Retry Protocol as a worked example of deterministic message handling. Its scope is a test receiver and sender, not a production network. The unique evidence marker is violet-cedar-427.

A receiver accepts a packet only when the payload digest matches the advertised checksum. The sender retains the same message identifier for retries. The trial rule permits three retries after the first transmission, for four attempts in total. The overall trial deadline is twelve seconds. These values describe the fixture protocol and do not establish any empirical reliability rate.

When a packet repeats an accepted message identifier with the same digest, the receiver delivers the payload to the application only once and sends its cached acknowledgement again. A repeated identifier carrying a different digest is rejected as a conflict. Counting four permitted attempts as four permitted application deliveries would therefore misrepresent the protocol.

Implementation notes separate checksum validation, identifier lookup, application delivery, and acknowledgement storage. The acknowledgement cache is checked before a repeated message can reach the application. The trial specification deliberately supplies no throughput measurement and makes no assertion about packet loss on public networks. Readers should preserve that limitation when summarizing the example.

# Message Delivery

## Meaning and boundaries
A stable message identifier and a checksum serve different purposes. [[wiki/sources/Acknowledgement Basics.md]] defines acknowledgements but supplies no retry budget.

## Evidence and limitations
Fixture specification (Harbor Retry Protocol): three retries after the first transmission give four attempts in total, within a twelve-second deadline, with the same identifier kept on every retry. A repeat of an accepted identifier with the same digest is delivered to the application once and answered with the cached acknowledgement; the same identifier with a different digest is rejected as a conflict. Four attempts are therefore not four deliveries. [[wiki/sources/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]

These are specified fixture values, not measured results: the source gives no throughput, reliability-rate or packet-loss evidence, and does not specify cache lifetime or post-deadline behavior. [[wiki/sources/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]

## Relationships
Complements [[wiki/sources/Acknowledgement Basics.md]]: that page defines identity and acknowledgement terms; the protocol page applies them to retries, and neither claims anything about real-network performance.

# Harbor Retry Protocol

## Summary
A synthetic specification by the Evaluation Standards Working Group (published 2026-10-15) for a test sender and receiver, not a production network. It supplies the retry budget that [[wiki/sources/Acknowledgement Basics.md]] leaves out. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]

## Key claims
Fixture specification (rules the protocol defines):
- The sender keeps the same message identifier across retries. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]
- The receiver accepts a packet only when the payload digest matches the advertised checksum. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]
- The trial rule permits three retries after the first transmission, for four attempts in total, within an overall twelve-second deadline. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]
- A repeat of an accepted identifier with the same digest is delivered to the application only once, and the cached acknowledgement is sent again. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]
- A repeated identifier with a different digest is rejected as a conflict. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]
- The acknowledgement cache is checked before a repeat can reach the application; four permitted attempts are not four permitted deliveries. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]

Limits: the values describe the fixture protocol and establish no empirical reliability rate; the source supplies no throughput measurement and makes no packet-loss claim for public networks. It does not state the acknowledgement-cache lifetime or what happens to attempts after the deadline. [[raw/clippings/Harbor Retry Protocol.md]]
